Issue #748

Essential Reading For Engineering Leaders

September 4th, 2026

Friday 4th September issue is presented by CodeRabbit

Fewer Findings But All Of Them Real. Only Real Risks Should Reach Your Queue.

AI writes more code than ever and a lot of that of ships with vulnerabilities.

CodeRabbit Security brings continuous code review and security into one AI platform, reasoning across your full codebase to catch complex bugs and vulnerabilities.

It's built for teams shipping at AI speed, where legacy pattern-based scanners can't keep up with AI-generated code.

Free trial includes 10 code scans.

Run CodeRabbit Security On Your Own Repositories Today

The Rise Of The End-To-End Operator

— Wes Kao

tl;dr: “At all types of organizations, I’m seeing more high-performers get rewarded when they can handle projects end-to-end. If a normal operator is an infantry soldier, these operators are Navy SEALs. They can parachute into unknown territory to quickly assess a situation. Then determine the best course of action.”

CareerGrowth

Load-Bearing People

— Mike Fisher

tl;dr: “Pick your most critical system, process or relationship and name the one person holding it up. Then ask what happens if that person is unreachable for a month starting tomorrow. If the answer scares you, write it down before the feeling passes, because these risks survive on the decision to think about it later.”

Management TeamHealth

Fewer Findings But All Of Them Real. Only Real Risks Should Reach Your Queue.

tl;dr: AI writes more code than ever and a lot of that of ships with vulnerabilities. CodeRabbit Security brings continuous code review and security into one AI platform, reasoning across your full codebase to catch complex bugs and vulnerabilities. It's built for teams shipping at AI speed, where legacy pattern-based scanners can't keep up with AI-generated code. Free trial includes 10 code scans.

Promoted by CodeRabbit

CodeReview AI Security

The Art Of Simplifying Decisions

— David Pereira

tl;dr: “For too long, we’ve endured complex decision-making approaches. Now that decisions are clearly our bottleneck, I’m bullish on those who can simplify them. I want to share my approach with you, and how you can bring it to your scenario. I hope this helps you simplify what others complicate.”

Leadership DecisionMaking

“A one-on-one is a place to listen for what your employee isn’t saying.”

― Michael Lopp

The Mistakes You're Allowed To Make

— Steve Huynh

tl;dr: My friend said something to me once that I’ve been repeating ever since: “Bad news delivered early is just called news.” I think about that line every time I make a mistake.

Communication CareerGrowth

More Than Half of My Candidates Use AI on the Initial Screening Call. Here Is How I Tell.

— Luka Biber

tl;dr: “I want engineers who use AI to write code faster. I do not want candidates quietly reading AI answers to questions about a language they have supposedly mastered over ten or twenty years. The initial screening call is where you find out which one you have.”

Promoted by Remgu

Management AI

The Safest Job From AI May Be Writing

— Murat Demirbas

tl;dr: While the programmer's job description is getting completely refactored, writing remains surprisingly unaffected. LLMs have gotten very good at generating code, but I am appalled at the absolute shit they spew as prose... I am increasingly convinced LLMs will not threaten decent writers anytime soon. My prediction rests on the three observations below. Tell me where my logic does not hold up.

AI CareerGrowth

Let's Build A Compressor From Scratch

— Adolfo Ochagavía

tl;dr: “Compression is one of those wonderful things we have grown accustomed to in the computer world. You wave a magic wand and — poof! — a file suddenly shrinks to a fraction of its size! You wave the wand again and — pop!— the original file is restored down to the last bit. How can this possibly work? Let’s find out!”

DeepDive Algo

Building Autonomous Goal Loops That Deliver

— Jarred Kenny

tl;dr: “The agent keeps moving, but movement is not the problem. The tests only protect what we already know, and the important failures sit outside them. A screen can look complete while it stores nothing. An agent can give the right answer for the wrong reason. A scorer can reward behavior no user wants. More turns make each of those failures cheaper and faster.”

Testing AI Agents

item.content:encoded:
Issue #747

Essential Reading For Engineering Leaders

September 1st, 2026

Tuesday 1st September issue is presented by Unblocked

The Context Layer For Modern Engineering Teams

Unblocked turns code, docs, tickets, conversations and production data into actionable context, so engineers move faster and agents stay on track.

Try For Free Today

Coaching Questions That Work

— Dan Rockwell

tl;dr: Some questions focus on situations. What happened? What’s wrong? What do you want? Begin with situations, but don’t park there. Coaching questions turn attention to the person. (1) What did you notice about yourself in that meeting? (2) What was going on for you when she said that? (3) What do you make of your reaction?

Management Coaching Tips

Modern Engineering Values

— Christoph Nakazawa

tl;dr: “I’ve been trying to wrap my head around engineering values and principles that matter for 2026 and beyond that will help individuals and organizations move faster. Looking at my engineering workflow it feels like on one hand everything changed, and on the other, not that much."

Management AI

[Webinar] How To Stop Babysitting Your Agents

— Brandon Waselnuk

tl;dr: Agents can generate code. Getting it right for your system is the hard part – you end up wasting time and tokens in the back and forth. More MCPs solve access but not understanding. Join us for a FREE webinar on Sep 2 to see how to give agents exactly what they need the first time (includes a live demo).

Promoted by Unblocked

Event AI Agents

How To Figure Out Your Next Career Move

— Cliff Maxwell

tl;dr: “In this post, I’ll help you answer six fundamental questions that will instill confidence and focus anytime you are navigating a transition at work. Each question comes with exercises and tools to help you build understanding.”

CareerGrowth Guide

“For things that you do not fully control, you should set internal goals rather than external ones.”

― James Stanier

Responsibility Is Taken Before It Is Given

— Lalit Maganti

tl;dr: “To get promoted as a software engineer in Big Tech, you generally need to show “ownership” of a product or area. This means being responsible for it and deciding what should happen over time.”

Staff+ CareerGrowth

How Laurel's AI-Native Team Ships More Verified Code

tl;dr: In three months, Laurel scaled agent-authored PRs from 55% to 76% of engineering output while cutting change failure rate by over 80%. Lightweight per-PR environments enable them to verify changes at agent scale and ship more code with fewer failures. Their ~60-engineer team now merges 2,300+ PRs a month. Take a look at their stack and what they implemented to get there.

Promoted by Signadot

CaseStudy DevEx AI

Bug Blindness

— Dan Luu

tl;dr: “I used to wonder why I see so many more bugs than most people. I easily observe hundreds to thousands of bugs per week and nothing seems to work, but most people I talk to don't see anything like this. For a long time, I thought this had something to do with how I use computers but, over time, I've realized that it's mostly that people are hitting the same bugs and don't notice.”

CodeQuality Debugging

Three Mistakes Of New AI Teams

— Doug Turnbull

tl;dr: “A surprising amount of the pain I see on AI teams looks very much like what budding search teams in the 2010s went through. Admittedly this gives me a biased perspective, but perhaps a useful one.”

Management AI

How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

— Michael Lynch

tl;dr: “I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

KnowledgeManagement Guide

Editorial Note

I'll be at LeadDev's LDX3 this September 15–16, looking forward to the conversations on how engineering leadership is changing.

I find it useful to hear from people doing the work and those that read this newsletter. If you're going too, I'd love to meet in person. Reply and let me know.

August 28th, 2026

Friday 28th August’s issue is presented by CodeRabbit

Review The Actual Change, Not The File List

Review Your Next PR With CodeRabbit Review Today

The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life

— Yew Jin Lim

tl;dr: “The best investment framework isn’t the one that maximizes returns. The best career strategy isn’t the one that eliminates risk. The best contemplative practice isn’t the one that promises instant transformation. The best framework is the one you’ll stick with. For me, that’s been a boring foundation with a laboratory on top.”

CareerGrowth

Elephants, Goldfish And The New Golden Age Of Software Engineering

— Dave Resin

tl;dr: “I argue that most of us are using our AI tools - including basic chatbots - wrong. I will propose a different approach that I hope will be valuable no matter who you are or what you do for a living. This section is for everyone and it sets up what follows.”

Management Productivity AI

Review The Actual Change, Not The File List.

CodeRabbit Review reorganizes any pull request from a flat file list into a structured, layer-by-layer walkthrough - the logical reading order of the change, not the order your platform happens to sort it. Every range gets its own plain-language summary, with sequence diagrams, state machines, and ERDs generated inline wherever a visual earns its place. (3) Code Peek lets you click any variable, function, class or type to see its definition and usages without leaving the tab. (4) Semantic Diff cuts past formatting noise to show what actually changed. From the team that pioneered AI code reviews. 2M reviews every week. 6M repos. 15K customers. Free during early access.

Promoted by CodeRabbit

Tools+Setup AI CodeReview

How Much Can You Hold Before It Breaks?

— Steve Huynh

tl;dr: “My optimal approach for a person has two parts, and each one addresses one of those problems. First, we want to pick a single piece of high-priority, high-impact work and protect it, so that whatever else happens, the thing that matters gets done. Second, we want to cut the number of things in flight down to as few as we can stand, so the switching costs are minimized. We want one thing at the top, and as little as possible underneath it.”

Management Productivity

“A good piece of written communication is the most effective means of broadcasting ideas and scaling yourself.”

― Will Larson

Three Resume Tips

— Sumner Evans

tl;dr: “In this article, I would like discuss the content of your resume. I’m going to describe three rules that I made up to guide your resume’s content.”

Tips CareerGrowth

Authentication And Authorization For Internal MCP Servers

— Paul Vatterott

tl;dr: Your internal MCP server can give LLMs access to everything by default, with no auth layer to stop them. This post shows how to lock it down with roles, granular scopes, and Enterprise SSO so employees and their AI assistants only reach the data they're cleared for.

Promoted by PropelAuth

Agents Auth Security

Making Your Data Ready For Agentic AI

— Prem Chandrasekaran, Pramod Sadalage

tl;dr: “Before any agent framework can produce useful outcomes, your data has to be in a shape that a machine can consume, trust, and act on. In this article, we discuss what your data needs to look like for agentic AI to derive value from it.”

AI DataEngineering Agents

We Need To Talk About Migrations With AI

— Gergely Orosz

tl;dr: “OpenAI put an impressive-sounding case study about how they helped Asana save $5.9M with a single migration. “Asana cleared 5 years of engineering work in 2 weeks with Codex. Using OpenAI Codex, Asana replaced an outdated testing system in two weeks for about $12K.” Gergely dive into this claim and discusses how migrations are changing.

TechDebt AI IndustryTrends

How We Saved 100 Terabytes Of Memory By Optimizing 1.1.1.1’s DNS Cache

— Sebastiaan Neuteboom

tl;dr: “Five successive changes to how cache entries are stored in memory cut the per-entry footprint by over 50%. Across our fleet, these changes freed up roughly 100 terabytes of memory, equivalent to the amount of RAM in 130 of our Gen 13 servers. The cache also got faster. Insert throughput rose 43% and lookup latency dropped 19%, as fewer allocations and better memory locality meant we did not trade speed for space.”

CaseStudy Scale Performance

Three Important Steps In My Maturation Process

— Thomas Dullien

tl;dr: So perhaps it is natural that I am reflecting on “what were the important realizations that I made since my early 20s that had a profound impact on the way I think about the world?” This post tries to list them.

CareerGrowth

“You manage things; you lead people.”

— Grace Hopper

You Should Never Be Angry At Work

— Sean Goedecke

tl;dr: “Healthy workplaces route around anger in the same way that networks route around damage. Emotionally unreliable engineers will get left out of conversations that might cause them to blow up. Decision-making will get done around them in backchannels. I’ve seen this become a self-reinforcing cycle: angry engineers aren’t consulted on key decisions, which makes them angrier, which pushes them even further away from the spaces where decisions get made, and so on.”

TeamHealth CareerGrowth

How To Give An Agent A Task Instead Of A Token

— Maria Paktiti

tl;dr: Give an agent an access token and it spreads: into the context window, into tool call logs, into notes it keeps between steps. Relay keeps the credential at WorkOS instead. Your agent names the user, WorkOS attaches that token and releases it only to allowlisted hosts, so a hijacked session is a live process you can kill rather than a token that works from anywhere.

— Farid Zakaria

tl;dr: “I have been probably obsessed with two things in the last few years: Nix as a tool to explore innovative ideas that require the capability to rebuild the world and replacing ELF with SQLite as an executable format. You might have noticed that these two ideas are well suited to each other.”

tl;dr: I wanted to make a blog post like this for a long time, because it’s something that I wish I could find more of myself. I think one of the things that helps us most in our careers as software engineers is knowing how to debug problems, how to reproduce them, and how to report them.

― Leszek Mazurek

Beyond Senior - Creating Hope

tl;dr: “This series explores what changes when engineers move past the senior level into staff and principal roles... This article is about why endings are so hard, what goes wrong when you don’t manage them deliberately, and how to land your projects well.”

Issue #741

Essential Reading For Engineering Leaders

August 11th, 2026

Tuesday 11th August’s issue is presented by CodeRabbit

Review The Actual Change, Not The File List

AI writes more code than ever. Reviewing it shouldn’t mean scrolling forty files in alphabetical order.

CodeRabbit Review reorganizes any pull request from a flat file list into a structured, layer-by-layer walkthrough - the logical reading order of the change, not the order your platform happens to sort it.

Every range gets its own plain-language summary, with sequence diagrams, state machines, and ERDs generated inline wherever a visual earns its place.

  • Cohorts group related files and chunks so you review one idea at a time.

  • Layers order them so foundational changes - data shapes, contracts - come before the code that depends on them.

  • Code Peek lets you click any variable, function, class or type to see its definition and usages without leaving the tab.

  • Semantic Diff cuts past formatting noise to show what actually changed.

From the team that pioneered AI code reviews. 2M reviews every week. 6M repos. 15K customers. Free during early access.

Review Your Next PR With CodeRabbit Review Today

Relentless Forward Progress

— Mike Fisher

tl;dr: “The hardest stretches of running a team are not sprints. They are ultras: the long downturn, the slow turnaround, the market that stays bad for six quarters straight. None is solved by a single heroic burst. They are survived, or not, by how you manage the long middle, when the adrenaline is gone and the only skill left is suffering productively while metering what you have.” 

Leadership Management Wellbeing

The Antithesis Principle

— Shreyas Doshi

tl;dr: (1) If you want to help people learn something, look into making it engaging / entertaining. This first one is the easier, more obvious conclusion. (2) It is actually not in your best interest to be the kind of person who can only learn from entertaining content. Nor to be the kind of person that needs any sort of entertainment as a prerequisite for learning. The vast majority of smart people will never consider this second conclusion.

CareerGrowth

Review The Actual Change, Not The File List.

tl;dr: AI writes more code than ever. Reviewing it shouldn’t mean scrolling forty files in alphabetical order. CodeRabbit Review reorganizes any pull request from a flat file list into a structured, layer-by-layer walkthrough - the logical reading order of the change, not the order your platform happens to sort it. Every range gets its own plain-language summary, with sequence diagrams, state machines, and ERDs generated inline wherever a visual earns its place. (1) Cohorts group related files and chunks so you review one idea at a time. (2) Layers order them so foundational changes - data shapes, contracts - come before the code that depends on them. (3) Code Peek lets you click any variable, function, class or type to see its definition and usages without leaving the tab. (4) Semantic Diff cuts past formatting noise to show what actually changed. From the team that pioneered AI code reviews. 2M reviews every week. 6M repos. 15K customers. Free during early access.

Promoted by CodeRabbit

CodeReview Tools+Setup AI

Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap

— Will Larson

tl;dr: “If you’re willing to embrace this fact that a little bit of time in middle management roles is important preparation to become an executive, but spending a great deal of time in middle management only prepares you for further middle management roles–and makes you less effective as a potential executive–then the AI-driven shift in managerial fads might be a threat to your current role, but it’s likely to improve your chances to succeed as an executive.”

Management CareerGrowth

"Let him that would move the world first move himself."

— Socrates

A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding

— Steve Huynh

tl;dr: “After nearly two decades at Amazon, operating as a Principal Engineer, often parachuting into complex, high stakes projects, I’ve developed a system to cut through this chaos. In this article, I’ll share with you that exact framework to help you get up to speed unbelievably fast.”

Management Guide Onboarding

Agents Can Now Sign Up For Your App

tl;dr: Agents hit your signup flow and bounce off a login built for humans. Every one that gives up is a signup you never see. WorkOS Agent Registration turns that traffic into signups. Enroll via the dashboard and AuthKit publishes an auth.md file agents read to register for scoped, short-lived credentials you control.

Promoted by WorkOS

Agents Auth AI

Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI

— Norberto Lopes

tl;dr: “There’s a lot of buzz that AI means companies only want seniors now. That there’s no room left for early career engineers. I don’t think that’s true. The thing actually worth worrying about isn’t whether you’ll get hired, it’s whether you keep learning in a world of AI, now that it removes the friction where that learning used to happen. And that, thankfully, is a choice you get to make.”

AI CareerGrowth

Agentic Code Quality

— Addy Osmani

tl;dr: “For much of human history, we’ve evaluated code quality via code review: someone reads what you wrote and makes sure it’s clean, thoughtful, fast, understandable, and tests well. For agents, that approach doesn’t scale well; there’s just too much code for anyone to read. As a result, more and more of our quality checks have to happen in the harness, environment, and operating system around the agent. Software quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents.”

AI CodeQuality Agents

Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases

— Gabor Koos

tl;dr: “This series is about making your programs more resilient. Each post looks at one part of the system we take for granted: networks, time, databases, storage, users, dependencies, deployments, queues, and concurrency. The question is always the same: what assumptions are we making here, and what should we do when they stop being true?”

Databases DeepDive

Editorial Note

I'll be at LeadDev's LDX3 this September 15–16, looking forward to the conversations on how engineering leadership is changing.

I find it useful to hear from people doing the work - whether they're running a small startup or a large org. It helps me understand the real-world challenges and how this newsletter can better serve you.

If you're going too, I'd love to meet in person. Reply and let me know.

Essential Reading For Engineering Leaders

The Context Engine For Modern Engineering Teams

Management ChangeManagement

Engineering Management After The Cost Of Code Collapsed

— Karim Jedda

tl;dr: “I still hear and read what I call the "old rules" repeated over and over: a director should not spend time coding, good work takes time, protect the team from the business, get consensus before you commit, etc...” Karim started checking each rule against the assumption underneath it after the introduction of LLMs in his org.

Management AI

[Live Session] Can You Prove AI Is Working?

tl;dr: AI is in your engineering workflow. While the token spend shows it, the throughput doesn't. The human is very much still in the loop, and that's a context problem. Join live on Aug 19 (FREE) to learn how to track AI productivity, how context maturity affects where teams stall, and what it takes to get real value from your agents.

Promoted by Unblocked

AI Events Metrics

The Conductor Developer

— Rachel Laycock

tl;dr: “A great conductor is first and foremost a great musician. They could play the instruments themselves. That’s not why they’re standing on the podium. Their value comes from understanding the whole score. The orchestra doesn’t need the conductor because the musicians aren’t talented enough. It needs the conductor because someone has to hold the whole system in their head. Increasingly, I think that’s what great software developers are doing.”

Leadership CareerGrowth

“No one cares how much you know until they know how much you care.”

- Theodore Roosevelt

My Agentic Coding Setup, July 2026

— Domenic Denicola

tl;dr: “Things are changing very fast, and I have no illusions that this will be a timeless nugget of wisdom. But talking to some friends and scrolling through X posts, it does seem that I might have some techniques in play that are not widespread.”

DevEx AI Agents

How Miro Builds And Tests Agentic Features At Scale

tl;dr: Miro's AI team was building a new AI architecture across nearly 250 microservices, and one shared environment meant tests constantly collided. With Signadot, they moved to verifying changes in parallel with lightweight environments in the cluster. Agents drive full end-to-end tests against live services and iterate before a PR opens. Engineers get verified working code without waiting for slots.

Promoted by Signadot

CaseStudy Testing Agents

Work Loudly

— Ben Balter

tl;dr: “In remote work, visibility isn't ambient anymore. If your work only shows up at the end - or only in your head and DMs—you make it harder for people to help, harder for managers to advocate for you, and easier for the org to miss your impact.” Ben shares his approach to working loudly.

Communication CareerGrowth Remote

The Bedrock of Software Design

— Alex Fedoseev

tl;dr: “Nothing has influenced the way I design software more than algebraic data types. It sounds overly academic—the kind of term that makes people roll their eyes or scares them away altogether. But honestly, it only sounds scary. The idea itself is quite simple, and learning it showed me a fundamentally better way to build software.”

DeepDive Architecture CodeQuality

Every Byte Matters

— Farid Zakaria

tl;dr: Farid argues that classic analysis isn't enough. The size of your data matters as much as your algorithm. CPUs pull memory in 64-byte "cache lines," so how tightly your data packs into those lines impacts speed.
